title: Book V: The Dead Hand — Chapter XLVI
paragraphs:
Pues no podemos haber aquello que queremos, queramos aquello que
podremos.
Since we cannot get what we like, let us like what we can get.—_Spanish Proverb_.

While Lydgate, securely married and in charge of the Hospital, saw himself battling Middlemarch for medical reform, the town was becoming increasingly aware of the national struggle for reform of another kind.

By the time Lord John Russell’s measure came before the House of Commons, Middlemarch had acquired a new political energy. Party divisions were sharper, and another election might reveal a clear shift in the balance. Some already predicted an election, declaring that the present Parliament would never pass a Reform Bill. Will Ladislaw repeatedly used this argument to assure Mr. Brooke that he was fortunate not to have tested his strength at the polls yet.

“Things will grow and ripen as if this were a comet year,” Will said. “Now Reform is on the agenda, public feeling will soon be as hot as a comet. There’ll probably be another election before long, and by then Middlemarch will have a few more ideas in its head. For now we need to concentrate on the ‘Pioneer’ and political meetings.”

“Exactly, Ladislaw. We’ll transform opinion here,” said Mr. Brooke. “Only, I want to stay independent on Reform, you know. I don’t want to go too far. I’d like to follow Wilberforce and Romilly—work for the emancipation of enslaved black people, reform the criminal law, that sort of thing. Of course I’d support Gray.”

“If you believe in the principle of Reform, you must be ready to accept what circumstances make possible,” said Will. “If everyone fights for his own little piece against everyone else, the whole cause will fall apart.”

“Yes, yes, I agree. I quite see it that way. That’s the light I’d put it in. I’d support Gray, you know. But I don’t want to upset the balance of the constitution, and I don’t think Gray would either.”

“But that change is what the country wants,” Will answered. “Otherwise political unions and every movement that knows its own purpose would mean nothing. People want a House of Commons weighted towards representatives of interests other than those of the landowners’ nominees. Fighting for anything less would be like asking for just a piece of an avalanche that’s already thundering down.”
“Excellent, Ladislaw. That’s how to put it. Write it down. We must start gathering documents about the country’s mood, as well as the machine-breaking and general hardship.”
“As for documents,” said Will, “a two-inch card would hold enough. A few lines of figures establish the misery. A few more will show how fast the people’s political determination is growing.”

“Good. Develop that a little, Ladislaw. There’s an idea. Write it up for the ‘Pioneer.’ Give the figures and deduce the misery, you know, then the other figures and deduce—and so forth. You have a way with words. Burke, now—thinking of Burke makes me wish someone had a pocket borough to give you. You’d never get elected, you know. We shall always need talent in the House, whatever reforms we make. That avalanche and thunder really sounded a little like Burke. That’s what I want: not ideas, you understand, but a way of expressing them.”
“Pocket boroughs would be wonderful,” Ladislaw replied, “if they were always in the right pocket, with a Burke always available.”

Will was pleased by the flattering comparison, even from Mr. Brooke. It strains human endurance to know you express yourself better than others and never have it noticed. When admiration for the right thing is scarce, even an accidental bray of applause at exactly the right moment gives encouragement. Will felt his literary refinements usually lay beyond Middlemarch’s perception. Still, he was beginning to enjoy thoroughly the work he had first accepted with a languid “Why not?” He studied politics as passionately as he had once studied poetic metres or the medieval world. Undeniably, without his wish to be near Dorothea, and perhaps his lack of any other plan, he would not now have been thinking about the English people’s needs or criticizing English statesmanship. He would probably have wandered through Italy, sketching plans for several plays, trying prose and finding it too thin, trying verse and finding it too artificial. He would have begun copying details from old paintings, stopped because they were “no good,” and remarked that cultivating oneself was, after all, the main thing. Politically he would have felt warm, general sympathy for freedom and progress. Our sense of duty often has to wait for work that replaces dilettantism and makes us feel that the quality of what we do actually matters.

Ladislaw had now accepted his share of work, though it was not the vaguely supreme achievement he had once imagined alone deserved sustained effort. His nature responded warmly to subjects visibly connected with life and action, and his easily roused rebelliousness helped kindle public spirit. Despite Mr. Casaubon and his exclusion from Lowick, he was fairly happy. He was gaining much new knowledge in a vivid, practical way and making the “Pioneer” famous as far away as Brassing. Never mind how small an area that was: the writing was no worse than much that travels to the ends of the earth.
Mr. Brooke could be irritating. But alternating between visits to the Grange and retreats to his Middlemarch lodgings varied Will’s life and eased his impatience.

“Move the pieces a little,” he told himself, “and Mr. Brooke could be in the Cabinet while I served as Under-Secretary. That’s the usual arrangement. Little waves form the large ones, following the same pattern. I’m better off here than in the life Mr. Casaubon would have trained me for, with every action fixed by precedents too rigid for me to influence. Prestige and high pay don’t interest me.”

As Lydgate had observed, he was something of a gypsy, rather enjoying the feeling that he belonged to no class. His position seemed romantic to him. He liked knowing that he caused a little surprise wherever he went. That pleasure had been disturbed when, during their accidental meeting at Lydgate’s, he sensed a new distance between himself and Dorothea. His anger turned towards Mr. Casaubon, who had predicted that Will would lose social standing. “I never had any standing,” he would have answered, had the prophecy reached him, color coming and going like breath beneath his transparent skin. But enjoying defiance is one thing; enjoying its consequences is another.

Meanwhile, the town’s opinion of the new editor of the “Pioneer” increasingly supported Mr. Casaubon’s view. Will’s distinguished family connection did not give him the advantage of an introduction as Lydgate’s had. If people said young Ladislaw was Mr. Casaubon’s nephew or cousin, they also said that “Mr. Casaubon wouldn’t have anything to do with him.”

“Brooke has taken him up,” said Mr. Hawley, “because it’s exactly what no sane person would expect. You can be sure Casaubon has damned good reasons for turning his back on a young man whose upbringing he paid for. Typical Brooke: the sort of fellow who’d praise a cat when trying to sell a horse.”

Some of Will’s more or less poetic peculiarities seemed to support Mr. Keck, editor of the “Trumpet,” in asserting that Ladislaw was not only a Polish agent but, if the truth were known, mentally unbalanced. That explained his unnatural speed and fluency whenever he took the platform—which he did at every opportunity, speaking with an ease that reflected badly on solid Englishmen everywhere. Keck found it revolting to see a slender young fellow with light curls stand up and declaim for an hour against institutions “already in existence when he lay in his cradle.” In a “Trumpet” editorial, Keck described his speech at a Reform meeting as “the violence of an energumen—a wretched attempt to use brilliant fireworks to conceal the audacity of irresponsible claims and the poverty of knowledge cheaply and recently acquired.”
“That was a lively article yesterday, Keck,” Dr. Sprague remarked sarcastically. “But what is an energumen?”
“Oh, an expression that came up during the French Revolution,” Keck replied.

This dangerous picture of Ladislaw contrasted strangely with other habits people noticed. He loved small children, partly for their looks and partly from affection. The smaller they were, provided their legs worked reasonably well, and the funnier their clothes, the more Will enjoyed surprising and delighting them. As we know, in Rome he liked wandering among poor people. He retained the taste in Middlemarch.

Somehow he had acquired a troop of comical children: little bareheaded boys in worn-out breeches, with scant shirt-tails hanging out; little girls tossing hair from their eyes to look at him; and brothers acting as guardians at the mature age of seven. He had led them on roaming expeditions to Halsell Wood in nutting season. After the cold weather began, he took them out one clear day to gather sticks for a bonfire in a hollow on the hillside. There he produced a small feast of gingerbread and improvised a Punch-and-Judy play with puppets he had made himself. That was one oddity. Another was his habit of lying at full length on the rug while talking in houses where he felt at home. Occasional visitors would discover him there, and such irregular behavior tended to confirm their suspicions of his dangerously mixed ancestry and general lack of principle.

His articles and speeches, however, naturally recommended him to families whom the sharper party divisions had placed on the Reform side. He received invitations to Mr. Bulstrode’s, though he could not lie on the rug there. Mrs. Bulstrode felt that the way he spoke of Catholic countries, as though there could be a truce with Antichrist, illustrated intellectual men’s usual tendency towards unsound belief.

At Mr. Farebrother’s, he became a favorite with the ladies. Events had ironically placed Farebrother on Bulstrode’s side in national politics. Little Miss Noble was especially fond of Will. One of his odd habits was to offer his arm whenever he met her carrying her small basket in the street. In full view of the town, he would insist on escorting her on a visit to distribute the little treats she secretly saved from her own share of sweets.

But he visited Lydgate’s most often, and spent most time on its rug. The two men were entirely different, which did nothing to prevent their getting on. Lydgate was abrupt but not touchy, and paid little attention to healthy people’s whims. Ladislaw did not generally waste his sensitivities on those who ignored them. With Rosamond, however, he sulked, behaved capriciously, and was often uncomplimentary, much to her private surprise. Nevertheless, his help with her music, his varied conversation and his freedom from grave preoccupations were gradually making him essential to her amusement. Her husband’s absorption in serious matters, despite all his tenderness and indulgence, often made his behavior unsatisfying to her and strengthened her dislike of medicine.

Lydgate sometimes subjected Will to awkward questions. He was inclined to sarcasm about people’s superstitious faith in “the Bill” while nobody cared about the poor state of pathology. One March evening, Rosamond sat at the tea table in a cherry-colored dress trimmed at the throat with swansdown. Lydgate, recently home and tired from his rounds, sat sideways in an armchair by the fire, one leg over its arm. His brow looked troubled as his eyes wandered over the “Pioneer’s” columns. Rosamond noticed his agitation and avoided looking at him, inwardly thanking heaven that she was not moody herself. Will lay on the rug, gazing absently at the curtain pole and softly humming “When first I saw thy face.” The spaniel, also stretched out but with little choice of space, looked between its paws at the intruder on its rug with silent, emphatic disapproval.
As Rosamond brought his tea, Lydgate threw down the paper and addressed Will, who had jumped up and gone to the table.
“There’s no point advertising Brooke as a reforming landlord, Ladislaw. It only makes the ‘Trumpet’ find more fault with him.”

“No matter. ‘Pioneer’ readers don’t read the ‘Trumpet,’” said Will, swallowing his tea and pacing about. “Do you think the public reads in order to change its opinions? We’d have a witches’ brew then, with a vengeance: ‘Mingle, mingle, mingle, mingle, you who can may mingle.’ Nobody would know which side to take.”
“Farebrother doesn’t think Brooke would win if an election came. The very men claiming to support him would pull another candidate out of the bag at the right moment.”
“It can’t hurt to try. It’s good to have MPs who live in the constituency.”
“Why?” asked Lydgate, fond as he was of using that inconvenient word abruptly.

“They represent the local stupidity more faithfully,” Will said, laughing and shaking his curls. “And the neighborhood keeps them on their best behavior. Brooke isn’t a bad fellow, but he’s made improvements on his estate that he’d never have made without this parliamentary ambition.”
“He isn’t suited to public life,” Lydgate declared contemptuously. “He’d disappoint everyone relying on him. I see it at the Hospital, though there Bulstrode holds the reins and drives him.”

“That depends on the standard you set for public men,” Will replied. “He’s good enough for the present purpose. Once people have made up their minds, as they’re doing now, they don’t need a personality. They only need a vote.”
“That’s typical of political writers, Ladislaw. You praise a measure as if it cured everything, and promote men who are part of the disease that needs curing.”
“Why not? Men can help cure themselves out of existence without realizing it,” said Will, who could invent reasons on the spot for questions he had not considered before.

“That doesn’t justify encouraging wildly exaggerated hopes for this particular measure. You help the demand to swallow it whole and send voting parrots to Parliament who can do nothing except pass it. You oppose corruption, but nothing is more thoroughly corrupt than persuading people that political hocus-pocus can cure society.”

“Very fine, my dear fellow. But your cure has to begin somewhere. Suppose a thousand things that degrade the population cannot be changed until this particular reform comes first. Consider what Stanley said the other day: the House has spent long enough tinkering with small cases of bribery, asking whether some voter received a guinea, when everyone knows seats are sold wholesale. Wait for wisdom and conscience in public officials? Nonsense! The only conscience we can rely on is an entire class’s powerful sense of injustice. The most effective wisdom is the wisdom of balancing claims. That’s my starting point: which side is being wronged? I support whoever advances its claims, rather than some virtuous defender of injustice.”
“Applying general statements to a particular case merely assumes what you have to prove, Ladislaw. Saying I favor the dose that cures doesn’t mean I favor opium for a particular case of gout.”

“I’m not assuming the answer to our actual question: whether we should attempt nothing until we find spotless men to work with. Would you follow that rule? If one man would get a medical reform passed for you and another would oppose it, would you ask which had better motives, or even better brains?”

“Of course,” said Lydgate, recognizing that he had been checkmated by a move he often used himself, “if we refused to work with the men available, everything would stop. Suppose the worst opinion of Bulstrode in this town were true. That wouldn’t alter the fact that he has the intelligence and determination to do what I believe should be done in the matters I understand and care about most. But that’s my sole reason for working with him,” he added rather proudly, remembering Mr. Farebrother’s remarks. “Otherwise he means nothing to me. I wouldn’t praise him for any personal reason. I’d avoid that.”

“Are you suggesting I praise Brooke for personal reasons?” Will asked, stung, turning sharply. For the first time he felt offended by Lydgate, perhaps all the more because he would have resisted any close investigation of how his relationship with Mr. Brooke had developed.

“Not at all,” said Lydgate. “I was only explaining my own conduct. A man can work towards a particular goal alongside people whose motives and general behavior are questionable, provided he’s certain of his own independence and knows he isn’t pursuing private gain, either a position or money.”

“Then why not allow other people the same freedom?” Will demanded, still hurt. “My independence matters to me as much as yours does to you. You’ve no more reason to imagine I expect personal benefits from Brooke than I have to imagine you expect them from Bulstrode. Motives are matters of honor, I suppose. Nobody can prove them. As for money and worldly position,” he concluded, tossing back his head, “surely it’s obvious that considerations like those don’t govern me.”

“You’ve completely misunderstood me, Ladislaw,” Lydgate said in surprise. He had been so occupied with defending himself that he had not seen what Will might infer about his own situation. “Forgive me for unintentionally upsetting you. In fact, I’d be more inclined to accuse you of romantically disregarding your worldly interests. On politics, I meant only a bias in your thinking.”

“How unpleasant you’re both being tonight!” Rosamond said. “I can’t imagine why money had to enter into it. Politics and medicine are disagreeable enough to quarrel about. Those two subjects give you both plenty of opportunity to fight the whole world and each other.”
She looked mildly impartial as she spoke, getting up to ring the bell and then crossing to her worktable.
“Poor Rosy!” Lydgate said, extending a hand as she passed. “Cherubs don’t enjoy arguments. Have some music. Ask Ladislaw to sing with you.”
After Will left, Rosamond asked her husband, “What made you so irritable this evening, Tertius?”
“Me? Ladislaw was the irritable one. He catches fire like tinder.”
“I mean earlier. Something had annoyed you before you came home. You looked cross, and that made you start arguing with Mr. Ladislaw. It hurts me when you look like that, Tertius.”
“Does it? Then I’m a brute,” Lydgate said, caressing her remorsefully.
“What had annoyed you?”
“Oh, things outside the house. Business.” In fact, it was a letter demanding payment of a furniture bill. But Rosamond was expecting a baby, and he wanted to protect her from worry.
